requirement: The IP client is optional; it carries IPv4 (RFC 791) and IPv6 (RFC 8200) over STANAG 5066 so that some IP applications can run over HF.
notes: Optional in Ed4 (U.9); it binds us only as far as we provide s5066-ip. Main 7.2 [p.12] lists the mandatory annexes, and U is not one of them.

requirement: The IP client normally sits with an IP router rather than an application or end system; the router may be co-resident on an end system, or an end system may use the client directly with an address on the subnet.
notes: Ours is the router model: the host's own IP stack routes into a tun device; addresses and routes are the operator's (docs/s5066-ip.md).

requirement: Under load TCP and HTTP are often unsuitable over the IP client; ICMP ping and low-volume UDP suit it.
An IP client can send and receive encapsulated datagrams with unicast IP addresses using both the ARQ and the non-ARQ modes.
An IP client may send and receive datagrams with multicast IP addresses using non-ARQ modes.
notes: Only when a group address is configured: interp U-0042.

requirement: IP datagrams travel in the U_PDU of S_UNIDATA_REQUEST and are delivered in the U_PDU of S_UNIDATA_INDICATION.
notes: shall (1). The annex writes U_DPU for the field; read as U_PDU, the name used in the rest of the paragraph and in Annex A.

requirement: No framing characters are added around the datagram, and none are allowed.
The first byte of the IP header is the first byte of the U_PDU, and so on to the last byte of the datagram, which is the last byte of the U_PDU.
notes: shall (2). The sentence runs on to U-3.

requirement: The datagram's bytes are bit and byte aligned with the octets of the U_PDU of S_UNIDATA_REQUEST.
notes: shall (3).

requirement: The least significant bit of each datagram octet is the least significant bit of the U_PDU octet.
notes: shall (4). Fig U-2 shows the mapping.

requirement: IPv4 and IPv6 are both carried; the version is the first four bits of the first header byte. The choice is transparent to the protocol, though a client may act on it.
An IP client binds at SAP ID 9.
notes: shall (1). Annex F Table F-1 agrees.

requirement: IP support is configurable to use either the ARQ or the non-ARQ delivery service.
notes: shall (2). The section has no shall (3): the numbering goes from (2) to (4) (checked on the rendered page).

requirement: The delivery mode and priority of each datagram are chosen from the type of IP address and from its contents, such as the protocol and the port.
A client may set the default service type of its S_BIND_REQUEST to suit the traffic it expects most.
notes: We bind ARQ: interp U-0039.

requirement: A client can override the bind's default service type and set the delivery mode of each S_UNIDATA_REQUEST, datagram by datagram.
notes: shall (4); the sentence runs on to U-4. Every request carries an explicit delivery mode.

requirement: Reliable point-to-point ARQ delivery is preferred for efficiency but in general cannot carry IP multicast, except where a multicast address maps to one 5066 unicast address.
Reliable IP delivery over ARQ uses: ARQ transmission, node delivery confirmation, in-order or as-they-arrive delivery, and a priority set as in U.8.
notes: shall (1). In order: interp U-0039.

requirement: If IP multicast groups are supported, the subnetwork is used in non-ARQ mode for them.
notes: shall (1).

requirement: Non-ARQ service may be used for unicast IP.
IP over non-ARQ uses: non-ARQ transmission, no delivery confirmation, as-they-arrive delivery, and a priority set as in U.8.
notes: shall (2).

requirement: For multicast the number of repeats of the D_PDUs may be more than one, for a better chance of receipt.
notes: multicast.repeats, the S_UNIDATA_REQUEST minimum retransmissions (S-0084); default 1 (interp U-0042).

requirement: In the router architecture IP addressing sits above 5066 addressing; the annex gives two ways to map IP to 5066 addresses, and a client may implement either or both. Talking to the router is an implementation choice, and the client may include the router function.
notes: The section starts on U-4 and runs on to U-5. We implement subnet-based mapping (U-0024) only.

requirement: Subnet-based mapping: the destination 5066 address comes from the IP subnet of the destination address, with an optional default mapping; this suits fixed IP routing.
notes: Longest prefix match over configured prefixes, then default_node.

requirement: Link-based mapping: the client is tied to a link to one remote router and that peer's 5066 address; this suits dynamic IP routing.
reason: optional mapping mode (U.6.3 lets a client implement one or both); we implement subnet-based mapping only

requirement: How the client talks to its IP router is an implementation choice.
notes: A Linux tun device (IFF_TUN, IFF_NO_PI); tests use an in-memory device (PacketDevice.cs).

requirement: Bridged architecture: both sides of the HF link in one IP subnet, the client mapping whole IP addresses to 5066 addresses; generally impractical.
reason: bridged architecture not provided: router model only (tun, not tap; decision of 2026-11-11, M0LTE.S5066 issue #116)

requirement: When IP arrives faster than the subnetwork takes it under flow control, a client may drop packets (simple, but costly with long HF delays and ARQ) or queue them (better, but long queues bring long delays); the choice is the implementation's.
notes: The section runs on to U-6. Our choice: interp U-0040.

requirement: Every Unidata carrying IP holds one complete IP datagram.
notes: shall (1). Nothing over the bind MTU is ever split: interp U-0037.

requirement: Segmentation and reassembly, if used, are usually the router's, but the client may do them.
notes: We leave them to the router: interp U-0037.

requirement: Client and router together make path MTU discovery (RFC 1191) work for datagrams marked Don't Fragment that are larger than the HF subnetwork MTU.
notes: Item 1. The tun MTU is set to the bind MTU, so the kernel answers locally sent and forwarded traffic itself; the client answers anything over the MTU that still reaches it.

requirement: ICMP is supported to provide MTU discovery.
notes: Item 2. IPv6 Packet Too Big (RFC 4443, RFC 8201) as well as IPv4 Fragmentation Needed (RFC 1191).

requirement: For each packet the client may choose ARQ or non-ARQ, priority, queueing and discard or filtering, from the destination address, the IP protocol and, for TCP and UDP, the port.
notes: The list of options runs on to U-7.

requirement: These per-packet choices are configurable.
notes: Worded as a recommendation.

requirement: Helpful considerations: ARQ usually beats non-ARQ; some queueing helps but very long queues do not; discarding traffic not explicitly allowed can help; control traffic such as ICMP is best at a higher priority.
notes: Items 1 to 4.

requirement: Changes in Ed4: descriptive text added; the annex made optional; IPv6 added; multicast made optional; DiffServ and TOS controls removed; address handling rewritten at subnet level.
notes: No TOS or DSCP based choice is made.

requirement: What the client does with a datagram over the MTU is NOT STATED beyond U-0029 to U-0032. Reading: never split it; IPv4 with Don't Fragment and any IPv6 draw an ICMP too-big with the bind MTU (IPv4 type 3 code 4 per RFC 1191, ICMPv6 type 2 per RFC 4443 and RFC 8201) written back into the device; IPv4 without Don't Fragment is dropped and counted, fragmenting being left to the router (U-0030). The answer's source is the original destination, which routes back through the device so reverse path checks pass. No answer to an ICMP error, a later fragment or a multicast source or destination; at most 10 answers at once and 10 a second (RFC 4443 2.4(e), 2.4(f), RFC 1812 4.3.2.8). A bind MTU under 1280 is logged as unfit for IPv6.

The default priorities are NOT STATED; only that ICMP is best higher (U-0035). Reading: priority 4 for IP traffic and 8 for ICMP and ICMPv6, both configurable, rules overriding either (priority 0 lowest to 15 highest, A-0063).
notes: Below HF chat's 12 (O-0014), so operator chat goes first.

requirement: The bind's service type and the ARQ delivery order are left open (U-0015, U-0018). Reading: bind ARQ with node delivery confirmation, in order, the most likely traffic; every request sets its own delivery mode anyway (U-0016). TTL is 0, the node's default.

The queueing choice is the implementation's (U-0028). Reading: datagrams wait in one FIFO queue while the node has flow off or the client is not bound; it holds queue_limit datagrams (default 32); when it is full the arriving datagram is dropped and counted (tail drop), so those already waiting keep their place. U_PDUs are sent without waiting for each confirmation, in order.
notes: Page U-5 to U-6.

requirement: What a client does with a received U_PDU that is not an IP datagram is NOT STATED. Reading: write it to the host only when it parses as one whole IPv4 datagram (valid header checksum, total length equal to the U_PDU) or IPv6 datagram (payload length plus 40 equal to the U_PDU); otherwise drop it and count it.

How multicast IP maps to a 5066 address is NOT STATED, multicast being optional (U-0005, U.9). Reading: IPv4 multicast (224.0.0.0/4), the IPv4 limited broadcast and IPv6 multicast (ff00::/8) go non-ARQ, as they arrive, to one configured 5066 group address with configured repeats (default 1, as interp O-0024); with no group configured they are dropped and counted. Received multicast is delivered like any datagram.

What happens to a datagram no mapping covers is NOT STATED. Reading: with no matching prefix and no default node it is dropped and counted (no ICMP unreachable). A default node that is a group address takes non-ARQ only, as the node rejects ARQ to a group (interp S-0138).

Whether filtering is on by default is NOT STATED; U.8 only says discarding traffic not explicitly allowed can help (U-0035). Reading: everything is allowed until the operator gives an allow-list; then only datagrams it matches (destination prefix, protocol, port) are sent. Filtering applies to what the host sends, not to what arrives from HF.
